extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and engineers working on LLM-based formal theorem proving, autoformalization, and Lean4 benchmark/dataset construction
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, autoformalizing, validating, and evaluating a large-scale Lean4 benchmark (FormalMATH) for LLM-based formal mathematical reasoning, including the human-in-the-loop pipeline, semantic/syntactic checks, disproof filtering, and prover evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic correctness via Lean4 compiler
rubrics_metrics.description: All candidate Lean4 statements must be syntactically correct and type-check with the Lean4 compiler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only syntactically valid statements are preserved for subsequent semantic verification; the paper uses a straightforward "compile-and-filter" strategy to generate high-quality training examples and to screen autoformalizer outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic alignment via multi-LLM verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic equivalence between the original natural-language problem and the Lean4 formalization must be confirmed by multiple general-purpose LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each LLM back-translates the Lean4 statement into natural language, compares the reconstructed description with the original problem, and issues a binary aligned/misaligned judgment. Only statements that passed semantic verification performed by all the LLMs are collected. This step filters out a large fraction (e.g., filtered 60.7% of syntactically correct but semantically misaligned statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-LLM group voting protocol (semantic verification prompt)
rubrics_metrics.description: The semantic verification process must follow a specified workflow: back-translate, check equivalence, and return a True/False judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The verification prompt instructs LLMs: (1) back-translate the Lean statement into English, (2) check equivalence with the natural-language statement, (3) return True if equivalent, (4) otherwise return False. The LLMs must return only True/False directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation-based disproof filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the logical negation of a formalized statement and attempt automated proof attempts on the negation; a successful proof of the negation implies the original statement is invalid in the formal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply transformation rules (e.g., De Morgan dualization) to construct ¬T and run off-the-shelf LLM-based provers to try to prove ¬T. Use this to identify inconsistencies and filter non-provable or misformalized statements; this strategy filtered about 1.6% of statements in FormalMATH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human expert verification (IMO-level annotators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final semantic fidelity is confirmed by manual inspection from high-expertise human annotators (International Mathematical Olympiad medalist-level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert reviewers to validate alignment after automated filtering. Annotation stats reported: 12 annotators, preservation rate 72.09% (from LLM-consensus stage to final retained statements), cost per statement $6.89, total duration 22 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble-based autoformalization with best-of-N sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate multiple candidate formalizations per example by running multiple autoformalizer LLMs and sampling (best-of-N) per model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For K autoformalizers, generate N candidates T_n^{(k)} per autoformalizer; first apply syntax checking, then semantic verification; repeated sampling increases chance of producing a correct formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile-and-filter training data creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Create paired natural-language/formal examples by having LLMs translate NL to Lean4 and keeping only those outputs that compile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields training corpora (e.g., 9,260 paired examples) used to finetune autoformalizers; compile-and-filter is a recommended practical strategy to bootstrap supervised fine-tuning data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pass@K evaluation metric for theorem provers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate provers by Pass@K: the fraction of problems for which at least one valid proof is found among the top K generated attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For BFS methods K = N × S × T (N attempts × S tactics per expansion × T iterations). For SPG methods, K equals total number of complete proof trajectories sampled. Use appropriate sampling budgets when reporting Pass@K (e.g., Pass@32, Pass@3200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proof-generation paradigms: BFS vs SPG
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between best-first tree-search (BFS) proof-search methods and single-pass generation (SPG) methods when evaluating and designing provers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BFS: nodes = intermediate proof states, use heuristic scoring and iterative expansion; SPG: generate full proofs in one pass (often using best-of-N). Evaluation, sampling budgets, and verifier integration differ by paradigm and must be reported accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting sampling budgets and their calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting results, explicitly state the sampling budget configuration used (e.g., 1×32×100, 32×32×100, Pass@3200).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling budget choices substantially affect Pass@K. Provide the mapping between search parameters and K (e.g., for BFS) and the effective computational cost, so results are interpretable and comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset composition and diversity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarks should cover a broad spectrum of mathematical domains (algebra, calculus, number theory, geometry, discrete math, applied math, etc.) and difficulty levels (high-school olympiad up to undergraduate theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FormalMATH includes 5,560 formally verified statements spanning many subdomains and multiple difficulty tiers; clearly report domain distributions and difficulty splits (e.g., plots, tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: FormalMATH-Lite curation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a tractable subset for scaling experiments, balance solvable and unsolvable problems and align domain distribution with the full benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FormalMATH-Lite (425 problems) is constructed by outcome-driven difficulty assessment (using existing provers) and stratified sampling to match domain distribution, enabling efficient test-time scaling studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier implementation efficiency (tree-structured parallelism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimize proof verification by centralizing expensive operations (e.g., Mathlib import) at a root thread and parallelizing per-proof child threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a tree-structured parallelism approach to avoid repeated heavy imports and to parallelize Lean4 verification across proofs to improve test-time efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompting strategies for proof generation (vanilla / CoT / NL-augmented CoT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different decoding/prompting strategies should be evaluated: vanilla (direct Lean4 generation), naive chain-of-thought (CoT) with explanatory comments, and CoT augmented with natural-language solution guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report each strategy's performance under the same sampling budgets. Empirical finding: naive CoT often outperforms NL-augmented CoT in Lean4 proof generation because NL guidance can omit low-level tactic detail and increase model perplexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: CoT prompt format requirement (explanatory comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: For CoT generation, prompts should request explanatory comments preceding each line of Lean4 code to elicit stepwise reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete CoT prompt templates; the paper uses prompts that ask for explanatory comments before each code line to encourage tactic-level detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: NL-augmented CoT caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Augmenting CoT with human-written informal solutions can harm proof success by increasing uncertainty and omitting necessary tactic-level steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical results: NL-augmented CoT increased perplexity and decreased Pass@K compared to naive CoT; report both success rates and perplexity metrics when claiming benefits of NL augmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify domain bias of provers
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze and report per-domain accuracy to reveal training or capability biases (e.g., algebra vs calculus performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide domain breakdowns (plots/tables). The paper finds provers excel in algebra and applied math but fail in calculus/discrete math; link these biases to training corpus distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error diagnosis and classification pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically analyze failed proofs via an automated LLM-driven diagnosis pipeline followed by human expert correction and classify common error patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-stage approach: (1) extract verbalized features/error indicators with LLMs, (2) assign error labels via a second prompt-driven call, then have humans review. Report major failure categories (e.g., missing constraints, incorrect goal logic, placeholders, redundant conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Autoformalization error pattern categories
rubrics_metrics.description: When autoformalizations fail, categorize errors such as missing constraints, redundant constraints, incorrect logical framing of goals (e.g., using ↔ instead of existence/uniqueness claims), and omission of required characterization (e.g., 'determine all tuples').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples of each error type and how they change the semantic intent; use these categories to improve autoformalizer prompts and post-filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require unanimous LLM agreement for collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Only collect a formalization if all semantic-verification LLMs return aligned (True) for that candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict consensus rule reduces false positives in autoformalization but lowers immediate yield; report consensus rates across difficulty levels (e.g., 30% unanimous agreement for high-school problems; much lower for undergraduate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation construction rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify transformation rules (e.g., De Morgan dualization) for constructing logical negations to enable disproof testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automate negation transformation consistently to feed LLM-based provers; ensure the negation is a valid Lean4 statement suitable for proof attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation rate reporting across pipeline stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the percentage of data preserved after each filtering stage (compiler checks, semantic verification, negation filtering, manual verification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use funnel charts or tables; FormalMATH reports e.g., 100% → 92.4% (compiler) → 32.7% (post-LLM semantic verification) → 21.7% (final). Also report the human-preservation multiplier (72.09%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training data provenance and diversity disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: List and disclose all source datasets and problem origins used to build the benchmark and training corpora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appendix/source list (e.g., MiniF2F, PutnamBench, OMNI-Math) and report how each source contributes to domain/difficulty coverage to allow reproducibility and bias analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting prover experimental settings and prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide full details of prompts, decoding strategies, and experimental settings (e.g., whether CoT/natural-language solutions were used, RL vs SFT variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include example prompts in appendices (the paper includes many, e.g., I.1–I.3) and state which models were trained with which prompting strategies to allow replication and fair comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report test-time scaling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing the impact of increased sampling (test-time compute), report performance changes across orders of magnitude of sampling budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FormalMATH experiments show limited returns for SPG with large sampling increases and better scaling for BFS but still costly; present absolute gains and computational costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensembling SPG methods: marginal gains expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When ensembling multiple SPG methods, expect small marginal improvements and report ensemble composition and combined Pass@K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document ensemble strategy (which models, how outputs aggregated); e.g., ensembling STP, Goedel, DeepSeek variants yielded only ~0.84% uplift in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt for domain classification (format constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain classification prompts must output a summarized sentence and classification chains using the given taxonomy, limit to at most 3 domains, use the exact chain format, and end with '=== report over ==='.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce taxonomy constraints (only last node may be 'Other'), separate multiple chains with semicolons, and maintain professional/report style—useful for dataset labeling and domain distribution plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier correctness: rely on compiler validation of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Lean4 compiler as the ground-truth verifier for proof validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat compiler acceptance as a binary success signal; because verifying proofs may be expensive, optimize verification (see tree-structured parallelism) and state exact verification procedure in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report failure modes and common prover error patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and report the main prover failure modes (e.g., reward sparsity, combinatorial search complexity, misuse of automated tactics, missing low-level hypotheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both automated LLM diagnosis and human review to enumerate failure patterns and provide illustrative examples. Use findings to motivate future algorithmic directions (intrinsic rewards, better exploration, alignment of NL->tactic spaces).
